prompt: In OpenVPN, what is TLS used for?
hint: Two channels, one of them TLS.

choices.text: Encrypting every tunnel packet as a TLS record
choices.why: The traffic goes in OpenVPN's own data packets, not in TLS records.

choices.text: Checking certificates and agreeing on keys
choices.why: Right. That is the control channel; the data channel uses the keys it produced.

choices.text: Replacing IKE on UDP port 500
choices.why: OpenVPN runs on its own port, 1194 here, and has nothing to do with IKE.

choices.text: Carrying only the web pages the laptop opens
choices.why: Anything routed into tun0 goes through the tunnel, web or not.

prompt: A rogue machine presents a certificate the lab's authority really did sign, for a server named files.example.com. Which line of client.conf makes the laptop refuse it?
hint: It is a genuine server certificate, with the wrong name.

choices.text: `remote-cert-tls server`
choices.why: That demands a server certificate, and this one is a server certificate, so it passes.

choices.text: `ca ca.crt`
choices.why: The same authority signed it, so the chain checks out.

choices.text: `verify-x509-name vpn.example.com name`
choices.why: Right. The name is files.example.com, not vpn.example.com.

choices.text: `dev tun`
choices.why: That chooses the kind of interface, and checks nothing.

prompt: What does `push "route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0"` in the server's file do?
hint: Push, as in send to somebody.

choices.text: Adds a route on the server towards the clients
choices.why: The server knows 10.8.0.0/24 from its `server` line.

choices.text: Gives clients a route to 192.168.10.0/24
choices.why: Right. The laptop's route via 10.8.0.1 arrived that way.

choices.text: Announces the office network to the ISP
choices.why: The ISP never learns a private network; the route lives on the clients.

choices.text: Lets the clients reach one another
choices.why: That is a different option; this route leads to 192.168.10.0/24.

prompt: In the lab's first configuration, the OpenVPN server listened on UDP port ___.
hint: The line after `proto udp`.

prompt: tshark labelled the laptop's Client Hello `TLSv1`, and everything after the Server Hello `TLSv1.3`. What happened?
hint: Look at what the log said was agreed.

choices.text: The client offered TLS 1.0 and the server upgraded it
choices.why: A server cannot raise a version the client never offered; the client asked for 1.3 inside.

choices.text: tshark could not decode the first packet
choices.why: It decoded it well enough to name it a Client Hello.

choices.text: An old version, written on purpose
choices.why: Right. The record header says an old version so old middleboxes pass it; the real one is named inside, and the Server Hello settles it.

choices.text: OpenVPN's reset forced TLS 1.0 for one packet
choices.why: The resets open OpenVPN's session and choose no TLS version.

prompt: Why could tshark not show the server's certificate in the capture?
hint: What did tshark call the packet after Server Hello?

choices.text: OpenVPN compresses it before sending
choices.why: Nothing was compressed; it was encrypted.

choices.text: It travels on the data channel
choices.why: The data channel carries tun0's packets, after the handshake.

choices.text: tshark keeps only the first 1264 bytes of a packet
choices.why: 1264 is the packet's size, not a limit of the capture.

choices.text: TLS 1.3 encrypts it
choices.why: Right. After the Server Hello it is inside what tshark could only call Application Data.

prompt: Match each message tshark decoded to what it was.
hint: Two of them are OpenVPN's own, two are TLS.

pairs.right: TLS starting inside the control channel
The rest of a TLS record, in another packet

prompt: Where did the laptop's route `192.168.10.0/24 via 10.8.0.1 dev tun0` come from?
hint: It is not in client.conf.

choices.text: The `remote` line of client.conf
choices.why: That names the server to connect to, not a network behind it.

choices.text: The home router's DHCP
choices.why: The home router knows nothing of the office network.

choices.text: The server pushed it
choices.why: Right. The `push` line of server.conf, over the control channel.

choices.text: It was typed on the laptop by hand
choices.why: Nobody configured a route on the laptop.

prompt: After the server's certificate, packets 9 to 11 went from the laptop to hq, about 2.7 kilobytes. What were they?
hint: The server checks somebody too.

choices.text: The laptop's certificate and proof, encrypted
choices.why: Right. The server checks the client as the client checked the server.

choices.text: The first packets of the tunnel's traffic
choices.why: Tunnel traffic goes on the data channel once the handshake is over.

choices.text: A retransmitted Client Hello
choices.why: Nothing was lost, and tshark named them differently.

choices.text: OpenVPN's acknowledgements of the server's packets
choices.why: Those are the small P_ACK_V1 packets, 68 and 72 bytes.

prompt: Behind the restrictive home router, the UDP client printed only `link remote` for eight seconds, and no error. Why no error?
hint: What does a drop policy send back?

choices.text: OpenVPN hides errors below log level 4
choices.why: Level 3 prints errors; there was nothing to print.

choices.text: The server rejected the certificate without saying so
choices.why: Nothing reached the server to reject.

choices.text: vpn.example.com did not resolve
choices.why: The line shows 203.0.113.2, so the name resolved; DNS was allowed out.

choices.text: The router dropped the packets and answered nothing
choices.why: Right. Silence, and the client kept waiting.

prompt: Which rule in the home router's chain let the TCP 443 tunnel start?
hint: The first packet of a connection is not a reply.

choices.text: `ct state established,related accept`
choices.why: That passes what follows; the first packet of the connection needs another rule.

choices.text: `iifname "eth0" tcp dport 443 accept`
choices.why: Right. The laptop's side is eth0, and the tunnel went to TCP 443.

choices.text: `iifname "eth0" udp dport 53 accept`
choices.why: That lets DNS out, which resolved the name but carried no tunnel.

choices.text: `policy drop`
choices.why: The policy is what blocked UDP 1194.

prompt: On a lossy mobile link, the same tunnel is far slower over TCP 443 than over UDP. What explains it?
hint: How many layers retransmit?

choices.text: TLS is slower over TCP than over UDP
choices.why: The cipher is the same; what differs is what happens on loss.

choices.text: Two layers of TCP both recovering from the same loss
choices.why: Right. The tunnel stalls everything behind a lost packet, and the TCP inside retransmits on top.

choices.text: Carriers slow port 443 down on purpose
choices.why: Web traffic is the last thing a carrier slows; the loss is the cause.

choices.text: TCP's header is larger than UDP's
choices.why: Twelve more bytes a packet cannot make a tunnel far slower.

prompt: What does a clientless SSL VPN portal give the person who signs in?
hint: There is no tunnel.

choices.text: A route to the whole office network
choices.why: No route is installed; the browser only talks to the portal.

choices.text: An address from the VPN's pool
choices.why: Addresses go to tunnel clients; the portal has none to give.

choices.text: Internal web applications, relayed by the gateway
choices.why: Right. A reverse proxy with a login in front.

choices.text: Layer 2 access to the office LAN
choices.why: That would be a tap device or VXLAN, and a portal is neither.

prompt: vx0's MTU is 1450 over a 1500-byte link. How many bytes does VXLAN put in front of the inner IP packet?
hint: The inner Ethernet header is among them.

prompt: Outer IP, UDP and VXLAN headers add up to 36 bytes. Why does vx0 lose 50 from its MTU and not 36?
hint: What does vx0 hand to the tunnel: a packet or a frame?

choices.text: The outer Ethernet header counts against the MTU
choices.why: An MTU counts the IP packet; the link's own header is never part of it.

choices.text: The inner Ethernet header travels inside too
VXLAN pads every frame by 14 bytes
choices.why: Nothing is padded; the 14 bytes are a header with addresses in it.

choices.text: The UDP checksum takes another 14 bytes of its own
choices.why: The checksum is inside UDP's 8 bytes.

prompt: The ping from hq to 172.16.0.2 through vx0 came back with `ttl=64`. What does that say?
hint: Earlier tunnels gave 62 or 63.

choices.text: No router stood between them
choices.why: Right. To the inner packet, the two ends share one segment.

choices.text: The ISP forwarded the inner packet
choices.why: The ISP forwarded only the outer one, and would have cost a TTL otherwise.

choices.text: The packet was never encapsulated
choices.why: The capture shows it inside UDP 4789.

choices.text: hq answered its own ping
choices.why: The reply came from 172.16.0.2, branch's end.

prompt: What is the entry `00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 198.51.100.2` in vx0's forwarding table for?
hint: The ARP request was sent to everybody.

choices.text: It is the MAC address of branch's real interface
choices.why: That would be a real address; this one is all zeros.

choices.text: A leftover that nothing uses
choices.why: The very first ARP broadcast went through it.

choices.text: Broadcasts and unknown destinations
choices.why: Right. It is the flood list: where a frame goes when no learnt entry matches.

choices.text: The default route of the network underneath
choices.why: Routes live in the routing table, not in a bridge's MAC table.

prompt: VXLAN carries whole Ethernet frames inside UDP, sent to port ___.
hint: The tcpdump filter in the capture.

prompt: Two offices share one stretched segment. Which of these cross the WAN? Choose all that apply.
hint: One broadcast domain.

choices.text: An ARP request at either office
choices.why: Right: it is a broadcast, and the capture showed one crossing.

choices.text: A DHCP discover from a new laptop
choices.why: Right: also a broadcast.

choices.text: The flood from a loop at one office
choices.why: Right: a loop's flood reaches every part of the segment.

choices.text: Traffic between two machines on the same switch at one office
choices.why: Their frames are learnt as local and stay on that switch.

choices.text: The ISP's own routing updates
choices.why: The ISP's network is underneath the tunnel, not inside it.

prompt: Put the start of the OpenVPN connection in order, as tshark and the log showed it.
hint: OpenVPN opens before TLS does.
items: Server Hello, with the server's certificate encrypted
Traffic on the data channel, AES-256-GCM
trap: The data channel's keys come out of the handshake, so no traffic can flow before both certificates are checked.

prompt: A customer's firewall reads the first bytes of every connection to port 443 and lets only HTTPS through. Will the lab's tunnel on TCP 443 pass?
hint: What is the first message of the connection?

choices.text: Yes, since anything on port 443 is HTTPS to a firewall
choices.why: This firewall looks at contents, not only the port.

choices.text: Yes, because the handshake is real TLS 1.3
choices.why: The TLS is wrapped in OpenVPN's own packets, after OpenVPN's reset.

choices.text: No: it opens with OpenVPN's reset, not a Client Hello
choices.why: Right. Port 443 only beats a firewall that filters by port.

choices.text: No, because port 443 is reserved for browsers
choices.why: Nothing reserves a port for a kind of program; the contents gave it away.

prompt: A manager wants the two offices on one subnet, "so it is simpler". Nothing needs the same subnet in both places. What do you recommend?
hint: What does a stretched segment share?

choices.text: VXLAN, since the kernel already has it
choices.why: Being available is not a reason; the broadcasts and loops come with it.

choices.text: OpenVPN with `dev tap`, because it is encrypted
choices.why: Encryption does not shrink the broadcast domain.

choices.text: Two subnets, routed through the tunnel
choices.why: Right. A failure or a storm at one office then stays there.

choices.text: Stretch it, with spanning tree running across the WAN
choices.why: That joins both offices into one tree, and one topology change reaches both.
